chapters.title: Chapter 16 · The Magic Art of the Great Humbug
chapters.artPrompt: a little old man in a green robe pouring bran and pins into a scarecrow's opened head in a glowing green throne room, a tin woodman and a lion waiting hopefully behind, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The Wizard was not a real wizard at all. He was a little old man from Omaha, with no magic in him. But his friends did not know this, and he wanted to help them. The Scarecrow came first. Oz took off the Scarecrow’s head and emptied out the straw. Then he filled it with bran, mixed with many pins and needles. “Now you have bran-new brains,” he said with a smile. “The pins will keep them sharp.” “I feel wise indeed!” cried the happy Scarecrow.
Oz fills the Scarecrow’s head with bran-new brains.

When the Scarecrow came back, Dorothy looked at him curiously. His head was bulged out at the top with new brains. “Why are those pins sticking out of your head?” asked the Tin Woodman. “That is proof that he is sharp,” laughed the Lion.

Then the Tin Woodman knocked at the door. “I have come for my heart,” he said. Oz cut a small square hole in the left side of the tin chest. He took out a pretty heart, made of silk and stuffed with sawdust. He put it inside and soldered the tin neatly in place. “But is it a kind heart?” asked the Woodman. “Oh, very!” answered Oz. “Never mind the patch. I shall never forget your kindness,” said the happy Woodman.
New word: courage — being brave enough to do hard things, even when you feel afraid. Oz said courage is always inside you.

Last came the Lion. Oz took down a square green bottle from a high shelf. He poured it into a green-gold dish. “What is it?” asked the Lion. “Courage is always inside one,” said Oz. “Drink it, and it will be courage inside you.” So the Lion drank it all. “How do you feel now?” asked Oz. “Full of courage!” said the Lion. He trotted back to his friends, feeling braver than ever.

That night Oz sat alone and smiled. It had been easy to please the Scarecrow, the Woodman, and the Lion. But Dorothy’s wish was harder. “It will take more than imagination to carry Dorothy back to Kansas,” he said to himself. “I must think of something quickly.”

chapters.title: Chapter 17 · How the Balloon Was Launched
chapters.artPrompt: a great striped green silk balloon rising above an emerald plaza, a little old wizard waving from a big basket beneath it while a girl holding a small black dog watches from the ground, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Dorothy waited three sad days. Her friends were happy, but she longed for Kansas more than ever. On the fourth day, Oz sent for her. “I think I have found a way to get you out of this country,” he said. “When I came here, it was in a balloon. I believe I can make another one. It can carry us over the desert through the air.”

“Are you going with me?” asked Dorothy. “Yes,” said Oz. “I am tired of being a humbug. I would rather go back and join a circus again.” So Dorothy took a needle and thread, and helped him sew. Oz cut the silk, and Dorothy sewed the strips together. First light green, then dark green, then emerald green. In three days they had a great green bag, more than twenty feet long.

Oz painted the inside with thin glue to keep the air in. A big clothes basket was tied on with many ropes. Then he told his people he was going to visit a brother wizard in the clouds. Everyone in the city came to watch. The Tin Woodman made a fire, and Oz held the balloon over it. Hot air filled the bag, and it swelled up big and round. Oz sat in the basket. “While I am gone, the Scarecrow will rule over you!” he called.
The great green balloon rises into the sky, with Oz inside and Dorothy far below.

“Come, Dorothy!” cried the Wizard. “Hurry, or the balloon will fly away!” But Toto had run into the crowd to bark at a kitten. Dorothy chased him and caught him at last. She ran back with Toto in her arms. She was only a few steps away when the ropes snapped. The balloon rose into the air without her. “Come back!” she screamed. “I want to go too!” “I can’t come back, my dear,” called Oz. “Good-bye!” And that was the last they ever saw of him.
Talk together: Dorothy would not leave without Toto. Would you have jumped into the balloon, or run after your dog first?

The people grieved for many days. But they said, “Oz was always our friend. He built this beautiful Emerald City, and he has left the Wise Scarecrow to rule over us.” Dorothy wept too, for her hope of going home had floated away into the sky.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 · Away to the South
chapters.artPrompt: a girl with a basket and her little dog walking down a sunny country road beside a scarecrow, a tin woodman and a lion, green towers fading in the distance behind them, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The morning after the balloon flew away, the four friends met in the Throne Room. The Scarecrow, who was now the ruler, sat in the big throne. The others stood before him. “We are not so unlucky,” he said. “The Palace and the Emerald City belong to us.” “But I don’t want to live here,” cried Dorothy. “I want to go to Kansas, to Aunt Em and Uncle Henry.” The Scarecrow thought hard, and the pins began to stick out of his head.

“Why not call the Winged Monkeys, and ask them to carry you over the desert?” he said. Dorothy ran for the Golden Cap and spoke the magic words. At once the band of Winged Monkeys flew in at the window. “This is the second time you have called us,” said the Monkey King. “What do you wish?” “Fly with me to Kansas,” said Dorothy. But the King shook his head. “That cannot be done. We belong to this country, and we cannot cross the desert. Good-bye.”
The four friends set their faces toward the Land of the South.
New word: desert — a wide, dry land of sand and rocks with almost no water. No one in the Land of Oz has ever crossed it.

Dorothy was ready to cry. She had used the charm of the Golden Cap for nothing. Then the Scarecrow called in the soldier with the green whiskers. “Glinda might help,” said the soldier. “She is the Witch of the South, the most powerful of all. She is good and kind to everyone. Her castle stands on the edge of the desert.” “The road is straight to the south,” he added. “But it is full of dangers.”

“I shall go with Dorothy,” said the Lion at once. “She will need someone to protect her.” “My axe may help her too,” said the Tin Woodman. “So I will go as well.” “And I will certainly go,” said the Scarecrow. “If it wasn’t for Dorothy, I should never have had brains. I will never leave her until she starts home for good.” “Thank you all,” said Dorothy gratefully. “You are very kind.”

“We shall start tomorrow morning,” said the Scarecrow. “Let us all get ready, for it will be a long journey.” Dorothy’s heart was heavy, but she was not alone. Her three friends would walk beside her all the way.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 · Attacked by the Fighting Trees
chapters.artPrompt: gnarled trees with long bending branch arms flinging a straw scarecrow through the air while a tin woodman chops a branch with his axe, a girl and a lion watching from a forest path, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Early the next morning they said good-bye to the Emerald City. The Guardian of the Gate unlocked their green spectacles and wished them well. “You must come back to us as soon as you can,” he said to the Scarecrow. “I will, if I am able,” replied the Scarecrow. “But first I must help Dorothy to get home.” Then the gate opened, and they walked out into the bright sunshine, with their faces turned to the south.

They walked all day through green fields and bright flowers. That night they slept on the grass under the stars. In the morning they came to a thick wood. It stretched far to the left and far to the right. There was no way around it, so they had to go through. The Scarecrow walked in front. As he passed under a big tree, the branches bent down and twined around him.
The fighting trees fling the Scarecrow, while the Tin Woodman chops back.

The next minute he was lifted from the ground and flung headlong among his friends. It did not hurt him, but it surprised him very much. He tried a second tree, and its branches tossed him back again. “The trees have made up their minds to fight us,” said the Lion. “What shall we do?” asked Dorothy. Then the Tin Woodman shouldered his axe and marched up to the first tree. When a big branch bent down to seize him, he chopped it in two. The tree shook all over, as if in pain. “Come on! Be quick!” he shouted. They all ran under the tree safely.
New word: flung — thrown through the air with force. The fighting trees flung the Scarecrow about.

Poor Toto was caught by a small branch and shaken until he howled. But the Woodman chopped off the branch and set him free. The other trees did nothing at all. Only the first row could bend their branches, like policemen of the forest. So the friends walked on through the wood without any more trouble.

At the far edge of the wood they stopped in surprise. Before them stood a high wall, smooth and white. It seemed to be made of china, like the surface of a great dish. “What shall we do now?” asked Dorothy. “I will make a ladder,” said the Tin Woodman. “For we certainly must climb over the wall.” So he set to work at once.

chapters.title: Chapter 20 · The Dainty China Country
chapters.artPrompt: a tiny shiny porcelain village on a smooth white plain, a little china milkmaid scolding beside a china cow with a broken leg, a girl in a blue dress tiptoeing past, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The Tin Woodman made a ladder from wood he found in the forest, and Dorothy slept while he worked. When it was ready, they all climbed up. The Scarecrow looked over the top of the wall first. “Oh, my!” he cried. One by one they sat in a row on the wall and stared. Below them was a country with a floor as smooth and white as a big platter. There were little china houses, china fences, and china cows and sheep and pigs, all standing about in groups. And the people were made of china too, even their clothes.
The dainty china people, small and shiny as teacups.

The tallest of the little people was no higher than Dorothy’s knee. They could not carry the heavy ladder up, so the Scarecrow jumped down first. The others jumped after him, landing softly on his straw body. As they walked on, they came to a china milkmaid milking a china cow. At the sight of the strangers, the cow gave a sudden kick. Over went the stool, the pail, and the milkmaid, with a great clatter. The poor cow had broken her leg, and the milkmaid had a nick in her elbow.
New word: china — thin, shiny pottery like teacups and plates. It is pretty, but it breaks very easily.

“See what you have done!” cried the milkmaid angrily. “I must carry my cow to the mender’s shop and have her leg glued on again!” “I’m very sorry,” said Dorothy. “Please forgive us.” But the milkmaid led her limping cow away without a word. A little farther on, Dorothy met a beautiful young Princess, all made of china. “Don’t chase me!” the Princess cried. “If I run, I may fall down and break myself.” “But could you not be mended?” asked Dorothy. “Yes, but one is never so pretty after being mended,” said the Princess.

Dorothy asked the Princess to come to Kansas and stand on Aunt Em’s mantel. “That would make me very unhappy,” answered the Princess. “Here we can talk and run about. On a mantel we could only stand straight and look pretty.” Just then a funny little clown came by, all covered with cracks. He had broken himself so often that he was mended in a hundred places. He stood on his head, and the Princess said he was cracked in the head too.

The friends walked carefully through the rest of the china country. The little people scampered out of their way. At the far side they climbed another low china wall. The Lion jumped last, and his long tail knocked over a little china church and smashed it to pieces. “That was too bad,” said Dorothy. “But we were lucky to do so little harm. They are all so brittle!” “I am thankful I am made of straw,” said the Scarecrow. “Straw cannot be easily broken.”

chapters.title: Chapter 21 · The Lion Becomes the King of Beasts
chapters.artPrompt: a proud lion standing on a mossy rock in a grand old green forest while hundreds of animals, tigers, bears, wolves and foxes, bow down before him, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Beyond the china wall the ground was soft and marshy, full of muddy holes hidden by tall grass. They picked their way carefully and came at last to solid ground. Then they entered a grand old forest, where the trees were bigger and older than any they had ever seen. “This forest is perfectly delightful,” declared the Lion. “Never have I seen a more beautiful place. I should like to live here all my life.”
The beasts of the forest bow down to their new King.

The next morning they heard a low rumble, like the growling of many wild animals. Following the sound, they came to an opening in the wood. Hundreds of beasts were gathered there—tigers, elephants, bears, wolves, and foxes. The biggest tiger came up to the Lion and bowed. “Welcome, O King of Beasts!” he said. “You have come in good time to fight our enemy.” “What is your trouble?” asked the Lion. “A fierce monster has come into this forest,” said the tiger. “It is like a great spider, with a body as big as an elephant. It has eight legs as long as tree trunks, and it catches animals and eats them.”
Talk together: The Lion still felt afraid, but he fought the monster anyway. What do you think real courage is?

“If I kill your enemy, will you obey me as your King?” asked the Lion. “We will gladly!” roared all the beasts. So the Lion marched away to fight. He found the great spider asleep among the oak trees. Its legs were long, and its body was covered with coarse black hair. Its neck was as slender as a wasp’s waist. The Lion waited until he was sure of his jump. Then he gave a great spring and landed on the monster’s back. With one blow of his heavy paw, he knocked the spider’s head from its body.

When the long legs stopped moving, the Lion knew the monster was dead. He went back to the opening, where all the beasts were waiting. “You need fear your enemy no longer,” he said proudly. Then the animals bowed down to the Lion as their King. He promised to come back and rule over them, as soon as Dorothy was safely on her way to Kansas.

chapters.title: Chapter 22 · The Country of the Quadlings
chapters.artPrompt: winged monkeys carrying a girl, a scarecrow, a tin woodman, a lion and a small dog over a steep rocky hill while armless little men shoot their flat heads out on long necks, red-roofed farms below, storybook illustration

blocks.text: They passed safely through the rest of the forest. Before them rose a steep hill, covered from top to bottom with great rocks. As they began to climb, a rough voice cried, “Keep back!” A strange little man stepped from behind a rock. He was short and stout, with a big flat head and no arms at all. Then his head shot forward on a long, stretching neck. It struck the Scarecrow and sent him tumbling down the hill. Laughter burst from every rock, and Dorothy saw hundreds of these armless Hammer-Heads on the hillside.
The Winged Monkeys carry the friends over the hill of the Hammer-Heads.

The Lion rushed up the hill with an angry roar. But a hammer head struck him too, and he rolled down like a ball. “It is useless to fight people with shooting heads,” said the Lion, feeling sore. “Call the Winged Monkeys,” said the Tin Woodman. “You can command them once more.” So Dorothy put on the Golden Cap and spoke the magic words. At once the Monkeys caught up the four travelers and Toto. They flew over the hill while the Hammer-Heads yelled and shot their heads into the air. “This is the last time you can summon us,” said the King. “Good-bye, and good luck!”
New word: summon — to call for someone to come, often with magic words. Dorothy summoned the Winged Monkeys.

The country of the Quadlings was rich and happy. Fields of ripening grain waved in the sun, and pretty brooks ran under strong bridges. The fences, houses, and bridges were all painted bright red. The Quadlings themselves were short and fat, chubby and good-natured, and they were dressed all in red too. Near a farmhouse the travelers stopped to rest. The farmer’s wife gave them a good dinner. There were three kinds of cake and four kinds of cookies, and a bowl of milk for Toto.

“How far is it to the castle of Glinda?” Dorothy asked the farmer’s wife. “Not a great way,” said the woman. “Take the road to the south, and you will soon reach it.” They thanked her and walked on. Before long they saw a beautiful castle, with three young soldier girls dressed in red and gold at the gate. “Why have you come to the South Country?” one asked. “To see the Good Witch who rules here,” said Dorothy. “Then come with me. Glinda will see you at once.”

chapters.title: Chapter 23 · Glinda Grants Dorothy's Wish
chapters.artPrompt: a kind young witch with red ringlets in a flowing white gown sitting on a shining ruby throne, smiling down at a girl in a blue dress who offers a golden cap, storybook illustration

blocks.text: First they were taken to a room to make themselves tidy. Dorothy washed her face and combed her hair. The Lion shook the dust from his mane. The Scarecrow patted himself into shape, and the Tin Woodman polished his tin. Then they followed the soldier girl to Glinda. The Good Witch sat on a throne of rubies. She was beautiful and young, with red ringlets, a white dress, and kind blue eyes. “What can I do for you, my child?” she asked.
Glinda the Good listens to Dorothy on her ruby throne.

Dorothy told her the whole story. “My greatest wish is to get back to Kansas,” she said. Glinda kissed the little girl. “I can tell you a way home,” she said. “But you must give me the Golden Cap.” “Willingly!” said Dorothy. “It is of no use to me now.” Then Glinda asked each friend what he would do. The Scarecrow wished to return to the Emerald City, where he was the ruler. The Tin Woodman wanted to rule over the Winkies in the west. And the Lion longed for the grand old forest, where the beasts had made him their King.
New word: grant — to give someone what they ask for. Glinda granted Dorothy’s wish to go home.

“I shall use the Cap to send you each home,” said Glinda. “First the Winged Monkeys will carry the Scarecrow to the Emerald City gates. Then they will carry the Woodman to the land of the Winkies. Then they will carry the Lion to his forest. After that the Cap will have no more power. I shall give it to the King of the Monkeys, and he and his band will be free forevermore.” The three friends thanked her warmly.

“But how do I get home?” asked Dorothy. “Your Silver Shoes will carry you over the desert,” said Glinda. “If you had known their power, you could have gone back the very first day.” “But then I should not have had my brains!” cried the Scarecrow. “And I should not have had my lovely heart,” said the Tin Woodman. “And I should have been a coward forever,” declared the Lion. “This is all true,” said Dorothy. “Now that each of them is happy, I should like to go back to Kansas.”

“The Silver Shoes can carry you anywhere in the world in three steps,” said Glinda. “Knock the heels together three times, and tell them where you wish to go.” Dorothy kissed the Lion’s big head. She kissed the weeping Tin Woodman, and she hugged the soft Scarecrow tight. Glinda came down from her throne to kiss her good-bye. Then Dorothy took Toto up in her arms. She knocked the heels of the Silver Shoes together three times and said, “Take me home to Aunt Em!” Instantly she was whirling through the air, faster than the wind.

chapters.title: Chapter 24 · Home Again
chapters.artPrompt: a girl in a blue and white checked dress hugging a gray-dressed woman in front of a small new farmhouse on the wide prairie at golden sunset, a little black dog barking beside them, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The Silver Shoes took only three steps. Dorothy stopped so suddenly that she rolled over and over in the grass. She sat up and looked around her. “Good gracious!” she cried. She was sitting on the broad Kansas prairie. Just before her was the new farmhouse that Uncle Henry had built after the cyclone carried the old one away.

Uncle Henry was milking the cows in the barnyard. Toto had jumped from her arms and was running toward the barn, barking furiously. Dorothy stood up. Then she found that she was in her stocking-feet. The Silver Shoes had fallen off during her flight through the air. They were lost forever in the desert.

Dorothy thought of her dear friends, far away in the Land of Oz. The Scarecrow was ruling the Emerald City, with his bran-new brains. The Tin Woodman was ruling the Winkies, with his kind silk heart. The Lion was King of Beasts in the grand old forest. And Glinda the Good watched over them all from her ruby throne. The Silver Shoes were lost, but Dorothy did not need them anymore.
Talk together: Dorothy saw many wonders in the Land of Oz, but she still wanted Kansas. What makes your home special to you?

Everything looked just as Dorothy remembered it. The gray prairie stretched away until it met the sky. No tree or house broke the wide, flat country. It was not bright and green like the Land of Oz. But it was home, and Aunt Em and Uncle Henry lived there. That made it the most beautiful place in all the world.
Aunt Em folds Dorothy in her arms before the new farmhouse.

But Dorothy did not mind her lost shoes. She ran toward the house as fast as she could go. Aunt Em had just come out to water the cabbages. She looked up and saw the little girl running toward her. “My darling child!” she cried. She folded Dorothy in her arms and covered her face with kisses. “Where in the world did you come from?” “From the Land of Oz,” said Dorothy gravely. “And here is Toto, too. And oh, Aunt Em! I’m so glad to be at home again!”
